title: 🔊 Sound Studio
description: Welcome to the Sound Studio! You are a Grade 7 student who has been chosen to set up the school's first Acoustics Lab. Over 14 weeks, you will explore how sound is produced, how it travels, and why different sounds sound different. From building instruments to measuring echoes, you will discover the physics behind music, speech, and noise. Can you master the science of sound and earn the title of Master Acoustician?
subject: physics
how_to_play: You are a Grade 7 student building and running the school's Acoustics Lab over 14 weeks.
Each week presents a sound challenge with choices that affect your knowledge, equipment, and creativity.
Watch your dashboard — your Studio Sections (Vibration Lab, Wave Tank, Recording Booth, Instrument Workshop, Analysis Station) are interconnected.
NPCs like Ms. Hertz (teacher), Echo (lab AI), Meera, and Vikram react to your decisions.
Random events like noise complaints and visiting musicians will test your adaptability.
Keep your Safety Rating high — loud sounds can damage hearing if safety is ignored!
learning_objectives: Understand that sound is produced by vibrating objects and needs a medium to travel
Relate frequency to pitch and amplitude to loudness
Measure the speed of sound in different media
Explain echoes, reflection, and absorption of sound
Design and build simple musical instruments using sound principles
Practice safe hearing protection during loud experiments
cultural_context: School acoustics lab, hands-on sound experiments, music and physics integration

rounds.situation: Welcome to the Sound Studio! Ms. Hertz strikes a tuning fork and holds it near your ear. 'Can you hear that? Sound is vibration — the fork vibrates, pushes air molecules back and forth, and those vibrations reach your eardrum.' She places the vibrating fork in water and it sprays droplets everywhere! 'See? Sound is physical energy. Let us explore it!'
rounds.goal: Understand that sound is produced by vibrations and needs a medium to travel.
rounds.coaching_moment: Delayed gratification: Understanding the basics of vibration now will make every musical and acoustic concept click into place later.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why can astronauts not hear each other speak in space without radios?
rounds.image_prompt: Grade 7 students in a sound studio, teacher striking a tuning fork near water showing splashing droplets, excited faces, speakers and microphones on shelves

choices.label: A. Sound is produced by vibrating objects and travels as a wave through a medium like air, water, or solid materials
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Sound is created when an object vibrates (like a guitar string, drum skin, or vocal cord). These vibrations push nearby air molecules back and forth, creating a wave of compressions (molecules pushed together) and rarefactions (molecules spread apart) that travels outward. This is a longitudinal wave — the vibration direction is the same as the wave's travel direction.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. Sound can travel through empty space (vacuum), which is how we would hear explosions in outer space
choices.feedback: 💡 Sound CANNOT travel through a vacuum! Sound needs a medium (solid, liquid, or gas) because it travels by making particles vibrate and bump into each other. In space, there are no particles, so there is nothing to carry the vibrations. Movies showing loud explosions in space are scientifically inaccurate — space is completely silent!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. Sound travels as a transverse wave, moving up and down like waves on the surface of water
choices.feedback: 💡 Sound waves are LONGITUDINAL, not transverse! In a sound wave, air molecules vibrate back and forth in the SAME direction as the wave travels, creating compressions and rarefactions. Water surface waves are transverse (particles move up and down while the wave moves sideways). Think of sound like a slinky being pushed and pulled, not shaken up and down.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: D. Only musical instruments and speakers can produce sound — everyday objects like books and tables cannot create sound waves
choices.feedback: 💡 ANY vibrating object produces sound! When you clap your hands, slam a book, tap a table, or even snap your fingers, the vibrating surfaces create sound waves. Your voice is made by vibrating vocal cords. Even rustling leaves and flowing water create sound. If it vibrates, it makes sound — though some sounds may be too quiet or too high/low for humans to hear.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

rounds.situation: Ms. Hertz plays two notes on a keyboard — a low rumble and a high squeak. 'What makes them different? It is the frequency — how many vibrations per second. More vibrations per second means a higher pitch.' She shows an oscilloscope displaying the waveforms: the high note has many closely packed waves, the low note has few spread-out waves.
rounds.goal: Understand the relationship between frequency and pitch.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Frequency is measured in Hertz (Hz). The human ear hears from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Understanding these numbers gives you power over sound.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does a guitar string make a higher sound when you tighten it?
rounds.image_prompt: Oscilloscope showing two different waveforms — high frequency and low frequency — student adjusting signal generator, lab bench with tuning forks of different sizes

choices.label: A. A higher frequency means more vibrations per second, which our ears perceive as a higher pitch
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Frequency is measured in Hertz (Hz) — the number of complete vibrations per second. A tuning fork vibrating at 440 Hz makes 440 complete vibrations every second, producing the note A. Higher frequency = higher pitch. The human ear can hear from 20 Hz (very deep rumble) to 20,000 Hz (very high squeak). A piano ranges from about 27 Hz to 4,186 Hz.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: B. Pitch depends on how loud the sound is — louder sounds have higher pitch and quieter sounds have lower pitch
choices.feedback: 💡 Pitch and loudness are completely independent! You can have a loud low-pitched sound (bass drum) or a quiet high-pitched sound (a whispered whistle). Pitch is determined by FREQUENCY (vibrations per second), while loudness is determined by AMPLITUDE (how big the vibrations are). You can shout a low note or whisper a high note.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: C. A guitar string makes a lower sound when you tighten it because the tighter string vibrates more slowly
choices.feedback: 💡 The opposite is true! Tightening a guitar string makes it vibrate FASTER, producing a HIGHER pitch. A tighter string has more tension, which makes it snap back faster when plucked. Loosening the string makes it vibrate slower, producing a lower pitch. Guitarists tune their instruments by adjusting string tension with tuning pegs.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: D. The unit of frequency is the decibel (dB), which measures how many vibrations occur per second
choices.feedback: 💡 The decibel (dB) measures LOUDNESS, not frequency! Frequency is measured in Hertz (Hz), named after physicist Heinrich Hertz. 1 Hz = 1 vibration per second. Decibels measure sound intensity (volume) — normal conversation is about 60 dB, a rock concert is about 110 dB, and the threshold of pain is about 120 dB.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

rounds.situation: Ms. Hertz turns the volume on a speaker from whisper-quiet to room-shaking loud. 'Same note, same frequency — but very different LOUDNESS. What changed?' She shows the oscilloscope: the waves get taller but stay the same distance apart. 'The height of the wave — the amplitude — determines loudness. We measure it in decibels.' She holds up a sound level meter.
rounds.goal: Understand the relationship between amplitude and loudness, and learn to measure decibels.
rounds.coaching_moment: Ethical reasoning: Sound above 85 dB can damage hearing permanently. Understanding decibels is not just physics — it is a safety and health responsibility.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do we measure loudness in decibels instead of just amplitude? What makes the decibel scale special?
rounds.image_prompt: Student holding a sound level meter near a speaker showing 75 dB, oscilloscope displaying waves of different amplitudes, ear protection hanging nearby

choices.label: A. A louder sound has a larger amplitude, meaning the vibrating particles move further from their rest position
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Amplitude is the maximum distance a vibrating particle moves from its rest position. When you hit a drum harder, the drum skin moves further, pushing air molecules with more force and creating larger compressions. On an oscilloscope, a louder sound shows taller waves. Loudness is measured in decibels (dB) — sounds above 85 dB can damage hearing with prolonged exposure!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. A louder sound travels faster than a quieter sound because it has more energy pushing it forward
choices.feedback: 💡 Loudness does NOT affect the speed of sound! A whisper and a shout both travel at the same speed in the same medium (about 343 m/s in air at 20°C). What changes is the amplitude (size of vibration), not the speed. The speed of sound depends on the medium and temperature, not on how loud the sound is. A thunderclap reaches you at the same speed as a pin drop.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: C. The decibel scale is linear, so a sound at 60 dB is twice as loud as a sound at 30 dB
choices.feedback: 💡 The decibel scale is LOGARITHMIC, not linear! An increase of 10 dB means the sound is about 10 times more intense. So 60 dB is actually 1,000 times more intense than 30 dB, not just twice! This logarithmic scale is used because our ears can detect an enormous range of sounds — the loudest sound we can tolerate is about a trillion times more intense than the quietest we can hear.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: D. Wearing earphones at maximum volume is safe as long as you do not listen for more than 5 hours per day
choices.feedback: 💡 Earphones at maximum volume can reach 100-110 dB — well above the safe limit! At 100 dB, hearing damage can begin in just 15 MINUTES, not 5 hours. The safe limit for prolonged listening is 85 dB. Doctors recommend the 60/60 rule: listen at no more than 60% volume for no more than 60 minutes at a time. Noise-induced hearing loss is permanent and cannot be reversed!

skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Standing by your values even under pressure builds integrity.

rounds.situation: Ms. Hertz claps her hands sharply and the class hears a faint echo from the far wall of the gym. 'How fast does sound travel?' she asks. 'In air at room temperature, about 340 meters per second. But in water it is 1,500 m/s, and in steel it is 5,000 m/s! Sound travels faster through denser materials because particles are closer together.' She challenges you to measure the speed of sound yourself.
rounds.goal: Measure the speed of sound and understand how it varies in different media.
rounds.coaching_moment: Risk tolerance: Measuring sound speed requires creative experimental design. Not every method will work perfectly — be willing to try, fail, and refine.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do you see lightning before you hear thunder? What does this tell you about the speed of sound vs light?
rounds.image_prompt: Students in a school field clapping two blocks of wood together, another student timing with a stopwatch at a distance, measuring tape on the ground

choices.label: A. Sound travels fastest through solids, slower through liquids, and slowest through gases because particles are most closely packed in solids
choices.learning_concept: Speed of Sound in Different Media
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Sound speed depends on how close particles are and how strongly they are bonded. In steel: ~5,000 m/s (particles tightly packed). In water: ~1,500 m/s (particles less tightly packed). In air: ~343 m/s (particles far apart). That is why you can hear a train coming by putting your ear on the rail long before you hear it through the air!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. Sound travels fastest through air because air molecules are light and can vibrate more quickly than heavy solid particles
choices.feedback: 💡 Sound is actually SLOWEST in air! What matters is not the weight of individual particles, but how closely packed they are and how quickly vibrations pass between them. In solids, particles are tightly packed and strongly bonded, so vibrations transfer almost instantly. In gas, particles are far apart and must travel a distance before colliding with the next particle.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: C. You see lightning before hearing thunder because light is produced first and sound is produced a few seconds later
choices.feedback: 💡 Lightning and thunder are produced at the SAME instant! You see lightning first because light travels incredibly fast (300,000,000 m/s) while sound travels much slower (343 m/s). Light reaches you almost instantly, but sound takes about 3 seconds per kilometre. Counting seconds between lightning and thunder tells you the storm's distance: 3 seconds ≈ 1 km away.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. The speed of sound in air is always exactly 340 m/s regardless of temperature, humidity, or altitude
choices.feedback: 💡 Sound speed in air changes with temperature! At 0°C it is about 331 m/s, and it increases by roughly 0.6 m/s for every 1°C rise. At 20°C it is about 343 m/s. Warmer air has faster-moving particles that transmit vibrations more quickly. Humidity also slightly increases sound speed because water vapour molecules are lighter than nitrogen and oxygen.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

rounds.situation: The class visits the school auditorium — a large empty hall with hard walls. Ms. Hertz claps her hands and a clear echo bounces back. 'Echoes are sound reflections — just like light bouncing off a mirror! But sound needs at least 17 meters of distance and a hard surface to create a distinct echo.' She explains how architects design concert halls to control reflections for the best listening experience.
rounds.goal: Understand sound reflection, echoes, and acoustic design.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Architects use sound science to design buildings where every seat has great acoustics. Science and design work together beautifully.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do empty rooms echo more than furnished rooms? What happens to sound when it hits soft materials?
rounds.image_prompt: Empty school auditorium with sound waves bouncing off walls drawn as arrows, student clapping hands, echo ripples visualized, acoustic panels on some walls

choices.label: A. An echo is heard when sound reflects off a hard surface at least 17 metres away, because the reflected sound reaches your ear at least 0.1 seconds after the original
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Sound reflects off hard, smooth surfaces just like light reflects off a mirror. For a distinct echo, the reflected sound must arrive at least 0.1 seconds after the original (the minimum gap for our brain to hear them as separate sounds). At 343 m/s, sound travels 34 metres in 0.1 seconds — so the wall must be at least 17 metres away (sound goes there AND back = 34 m).

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. Echoes are caused by the wind carrying your voice back to you, which is why echoes are louder on windy days
choices.feedback: 💡 Echoes have nothing to do with wind! An echo is sound REFLECTING off a hard surface, just like a ball bouncing off a wall. The sound wave hits the surface and bounces back toward you. Wind can affect how sound carries over distance, but echoes work by reflection — they happen even in perfectly still air inside buildings.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. Soft materials like curtains and carpets make echoes louder because they amplify the sound waves that bounce off them
choices.feedback: 💡 Soft materials ABSORB sound rather than reflecting it, which REDUCES echoes! That is why empty rooms echo (hard walls reflect sound) while furnished rooms do not (furniture, carpets, and curtains absorb sound energy). Concert halls use a careful mix of reflective and absorbent surfaces to create the best acoustics.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: D. Bats can see in the dark using their excellent night vision, not sound waves
choices.feedback: 💡 Most bats actually have poor eyesight and navigate using ECHOLOCATION — they emit high-frequency ultrasonic clicks (up to 200 per second!) and listen for the echoes bouncing off objects. By analyzing the timing and direction of echoes, bats build a detailed 'sound map' of their surroundings. Dolphins and submarines use the same principle (sonar)!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

rounds.situation: Project week! Ms. Hertz announces: 'Use everything you know about frequency, amplitude, vibration, and resonance to design and build a musical instrument from scratch. It must play at least 5 different notes and you must be able to explain the physics behind every sound it makes.' Meera is already sketching ideas. Vikram is calculating frequencies.
rounds.goal: Design and build a working musical instrument using sound physics principles.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: Building an instrument requires combining knowledge (which notes?), skill (how to build?), and creativity (how to make it unique). This is engineering at its best.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How does understanding the physics of sound make you a BETTER instrument designer, not just a better scientist?
rounds.image_prompt: Student building a xylophone from water glasses at different fill levels, homemade pan flute and rubber band guitar also on table, colorful creative workspace

choices.label: A. A shorter vibrating string or air column produces a higher pitch because it vibrates at a higher frequency
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Shorter vibrating objects vibrate faster (higher frequency = higher pitch). This is why pressing a guitar fret shortens the string and raises the pitch. In wind instruments, shorter air columns produce higher notes — a piccolo (short) plays higher than a tuba (long). On a xylophone, shorter bars produce higher notes. Length is the most fundamental way to control pitch!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.
skill_explanation.creativity: Looking at the problem from a new angle demonstrates creativity.

choices.label: B. In a wind instrument like a flute, sound is produced by the air inside the tube being heated by the player's breath
choices.feedback: 💡 Sound in wind instruments comes from VIBRATING AIR COLUMNS, not heated air! When you blow across a flute's mouthpiece, the air stream splits and creates vibrations in the air column inside the tube. The length of the vibrating air column (controlled by covering holes) determines the pitch. Temperature plays no significant role in the sound production.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: C. All string instruments must be made of wood because only wood can vibrate at musical frequencies
choices.feedback: 💡 Any material can vibrate at musical frequencies! Metal strings, plastic strings, rubber bands, and even water glasses can all produce musical notes. Wood is used for guitar bodies and violin bodies not because it vibrates at special frequencies, but because it resonates and amplifies the sound beautifully. The body acts as an amplifier, not the primary vibrator.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: D. A drum produces different pitches by hitting it in different locations — the centre always gives the highest pitch
choices.feedback: 💡 Hitting different spots on a drum changes the timbre (tone quality) more than the pitch. The centre gives a fuller, deeper tone while the edge gives a higher, sharper sound, but the main pitch depends on the drum SIZE, skin TENSION, and skin THICKNESS. To change a drum's pitch significantly, you tighten or loosen the skin using the tuning lugs around the rim.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

rounds.situation: EMERGENCY! During a loud experiment, feedback from a microphone creates an ear-splitting screech at maximum volume. Several students grab their ears in pain, and one student complains of ringing in their ears (tinnitus) that will not stop. Ms. Hertz immediately turns off all equipment and checks on everyone. 'This is exactly why I stress hearing safety,' she says seriously.
rounds.goal: Handle a hearing safety emergency and strengthen safety protocols.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Unlike cuts and bruises, hearing damage is invisible and often permanent. This crisis teaches a lesson about invisible risks that applies far beyond the lab.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why is hearing damage scarier than most injuries? What makes it different from a cut or a burn?
rounds.image_prompt: Students in a sound studio covering their ears, one student looking distressed with ringing sensation illustrated as circles around head, teacher rushing to turn off speaker

choices.label: A. Prolonged exposure to sounds above 85 dB can cause permanent hearing damage because it destroys the tiny hair cells in the inner ear (cochlea)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Inside your cochlea (inner ear) are about 15,000 tiny hair cells that convert sound vibrations into electrical signals for your brain. Loud sounds (above 85 dB) can bend and break these delicate hair cells. Once damaged, they NEVER regenerate in humans — hearing loss is permanent. This is why ear protection is mandatory in loud environments!

skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Thinking about what's fair for everyone involved shows ethical awareness.

choices.label: B. Your ears can fully recover from loud noise damage if you rest them for a few days, similar to how muscles recover after exercise
choices.feedback: 💡 Extremely dangerous misconception! While temporary ringing (tinnitus) after a loud concert may fade, the underlying damage to hair cells in your cochlea is PERMANENT. Unlike muscles, ear hair cells do NOT regenerate in humans. Each exposure to loud noise kills more hair cells, and the damage accumulates over your lifetime. Prevention is the ONLY solution.

skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Choosing what's right over what's easy shows moral courage.

choices.label: C. Hearing damage only happens to elderly people — young people's ears are naturally protected from loud sounds
choices.feedback: 💡 Young people are equally vulnerable to noise damage! In fact, studies show hearing loss among teenagers has increased by 30% due to earphone use. The WHO warns that 1.1 billion young people are at risk. Your ears have no age-related protection — the same volume that damages a 60-year-old's hearing will damage a 12-year-old's too.

skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Considering fairness in your decision demonstrates ethical thinking.

choices.label: D. Tinnitus (ringing in the ears) is just a minor annoyance that has no connection to actual hearing damage
choices.feedback: 💡 Tinnitus is often a WARNING SIGN of hearing damage! The ringing or buzzing happens when damaged hair cells in your cochlea send false signals to your brain. While temporary tinnitus may fade, repeated episodes indicate cumulative damage. Some people develop permanent tinnitus that never stops — imagine hearing a constant ringing sound 24/7 for the rest of your life.

skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Weighing the ethical implications shows principled reasoning.

rounds.round_title: Week 8: Resonance — The Power of Matching
rounds.situation: Ms. Hertz holds two identical tuning forks. She strikes one and holds it near the other — and the second fork starts vibrating on its own! 'This is resonance — when an object vibrates at its natural frequency, even a small push can create huge vibrations.' She shows a video of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge, which collapsed because wind matched its resonance frequency.
rounds.goal: Understand resonance, natural frequency, and forced vibration.
rounds.coaching_moment: Adaptability: Resonance shows that timing matters more than force. A small push at the right moment is more powerful than a big push at the wrong moment — true in physics and in life.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How is pushing someone on a swing an example of resonance? What happens if you push at the wrong moment?
rounds.image_prompt: Two tuning forks facing each other, one struck and vibrating with sound waves reaching the second one which also vibrates, resonance diagram on whiteboard

choices.label: A. Resonance occurs when an object is forced to vibrate at its natural frequency, causing the vibrations to build up to a very large amplitude
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Every object has a natural frequency at which it 'wants' to vibrate. When an external force pushes the object at this exact frequency, each push adds to the previous vibration (like pushing a swing at the right moment). The amplitude grows dramatically — this is resonance. A wine glass can shatter if a singer hits its exact resonant frequency because the vibrations become so large!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. Resonance only happens with sound waves — it cannot occur with mechanical objects like bridges or buildings
choices.feedback: 💡 Resonance happens with ANY vibrating system! The Tacoma Narrows Bridge famously collapsed in 1940 because wind gusts matched its resonant frequency, causing it to vibrate with increasing amplitude until it tore apart. Soldiers break step when crossing bridges to avoid resonance. Earthquakes can cause resonance in buildings. It is a universal physics phenomenon!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: C. When you push a swing, it goes higher if you push at random times because unpredictable pushes create stronger vibrations
choices.feedback: 💡 Random pushes actually REDUCE swing amplitude! For maximum height, you must push at exactly the right moment — at the natural frequency of the swing. Each well-timed push adds energy to the motion (resonance). Pushing at random times sometimes adds energy and sometimes takes it away, resulting in smaller overall swings. This is the fundamental principle of resonance: timing matters more than force!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: D. A tuning fork only vibrates when struck — it cannot start vibrating from sound waves produced by another tuning fork nearby
choices.feedback: 💡 This is exactly what resonance does! If two identical tuning forks (same frequency) are placed near each other and one is struck, the sound waves will cause the second fork to start vibrating ON ITS OWN. This is called sympathetic resonance — the sound waves from the first fork push the second fork at its natural frequency, building up vibrations.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

rounds.situation: Ms. Hertz fills a long metal pipe, a water tank, and an air tube with speakers at one end and microphones at the other. 'Sound behaves differently in solids, liquids, and gases because the particles are packed differently,' she explains. 'Today we test how sound speed, quality, and behavior change across media.' She also mentions that sound cannot travel through a vacuum — no particles, no sound!
rounds.goal: Compare how sound travels through solids, liquids, and gases.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Understanding how medium affects sound explains everything from submarine sonar to why you can hear better with your ear against a wall.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why can whales communicate over hundreds of kilometers in water, but we can only hear a shout across a few hundred meters in air?
rounds.image_prompt: Three experimental setups side by side — speaker through metal rod, through water tank, through air tube — student measuring sound arrival times at each

choices.label: A. Sound cannot travel through a vacuum because there are no particles to vibrate and pass the wave energy along
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Sound is a mechanical wave that needs particles to travel. When air is pumped out of a glass bell jar containing a ringing bell, the sound fades to silence even though you can SEE the bell still ringing. This classic experiment proves that no particles = no sound. In outer space (nearly a perfect vacuum), astronauts cannot hear each other without radios!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. Sound travels at the same speed in all materials because the frequency of the vibration determines the speed
choices.feedback: 💡 Sound speed varies enormously between materials! In air: ~343 m/s. In water: ~1,500 m/s. In steel: ~5,000 m/s. The speed depends on how closely packed the particles are and how rigid the material is, NOT on frequency. Frequency stays the same as sound passes between media, but speed and wavelength change.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: C. Whales can communicate over hundreds of kilometres in water because water amplifies sound, making it louder over distance
choices.feedback: 💡 Water does not amplify sound — sound still loses energy over distance in water. However, sound travels much more EFFICIENTLY in water because water molecules are packed closely together and transmit vibrations with less energy loss than air. Also, certain ocean layers (the SOFAR channel) act as sound guides, trapping and channeling sound over vast distances.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. Putting your ear against a table to hear tapping on the other end does not work because solid surfaces block sound waves
choices.feedback: 💡 It actually works brilliantly! Sound travels FASTER and more efficiently through solids than through air. When you put your ear on a table and someone taps the other end, the vibrations travel through the tightly-packed particles in the wood and reach your ear before the airborne sound does. Native Americans famously listened for approaching horses by putting their ears to the ground.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

rounds.situation: Ms. Hertz plucks a guitar string and shows the oscilloscope. 'See how the wave is not a simple sine wave? That is because a vibrating string does not just vibrate as a whole — it also vibrates in halves, thirds, and quarters simultaneously! These are harmonics.' She shows how the same note on a piano and a violin have the same fundamental frequency but different harmonics — that is what gives each instrument its unique sound or 'timbre.'
rounds.goal: Understand harmonics, overtones, and why different instruments sound different.
rounds.coaching_moment: Ethical reasoning: Music is math made audible. The harmonics of a string follow perfect mathematical ratios — this connects beauty to precision.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does a violin playing the same note as a trumpet sound completely different? What role do harmonics play?
rounds.image_prompt: Oscilloscope showing complex waveform decomposed into fundamental and harmonic frequencies, student comparing waveforms of guitar and flute playing same note

choices.label: A. A violin and a flute playing the same note sound different because each instrument produces a unique pattern of harmonics (overtones) above the fundamental frequency
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ When a string or air column vibrates, it does not just vibrate as a whole (fundamental frequency). It also vibrates in halves (2nd harmonic), thirds (3rd harmonic), and so on. The unique MIX of these harmonics is called timbre. A flute produces almost a pure fundamental with few harmonics (clean sound), while a violin has rich, complex harmonics (warm, full sound). Same note, different 'fingerprint'!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. A violin and a flute playing the same note produce exactly identical sound waves that look the same on an oscilloscope
choices.feedback: 💡 They have the same fundamental frequency but very DIFFERENT waveforms! On an oscilloscope, a flute shows a nearly smooth sine wave, while a violin shows a complex, jagged wave. The difference is in the harmonics — the extra frequencies layered on top of the fundamental. This is why we can tell instruments apart even when they play the same note.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: C. Harmonics are sounds at random frequencies that are produced by imperfections in the instrument's construction
choices.feedback: 💡 Harmonics are NOT random — they follow a precise mathematical pattern! If the fundamental frequency is f, the harmonics are 2f, 3f, 4f, 5f, and so on (whole number multiples). For a string playing A at 440 Hz, the harmonics are 880 Hz, 1320 Hz, 1760 Hz, etc. This mathematical relationship is why music sounds 'harmonious' — it is physics and mathematics creating beauty!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. An octave is the gap between any two musical notes, and all note gaps are called octaves
choices.feedback: 💡 An octave is a very specific interval — it is the gap between a note and another note at EXACTLY DOUBLE the frequency. Middle C is 262 Hz; the C one octave higher is 524 Hz (2 × 262). The 2:1 ratio is why notes an octave apart sound 'the same but higher.' Other intervals have different frequency ratios: a perfect fifth is 3:2, a perfect fourth is 4:3.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

rounds.situation: Ms. Hertz announces a team competition: 'Each team will design, build, and perform with a set of homemade instruments that demonstrate at least three sound physics principles. You will explain the science behind every sound you make. Best performance wins the Golden Ear trophy!' Meera is already humming melodies. Vikram is sketching instrument designs.
rounds.goal: Collaborate to build a set of instruments and create a physics-based musical performance.
rounds.coaching_moment: Empathy: A great musical performance requires listening — to each other and to the science. Teams that communicate well produce the most harmonious results.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How is a team project like an orchestra? What happens when one person is out of tune with the rest?
rounds.image_prompt: Team of students building and testing homemade instruments together, one tuning water glasses, one cutting tubes, one testing with oscilloscope, creative teamwork

choices.label: A. A water glass xylophone works because different water levels change the mass of the vibrating system — more water means slower vibrations and lower pitch
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ When you tap a water glass, the glass walls vibrate. Adding water increases the total vibrating mass, which slows the vibration and lowers the pitch. More water = lower pitch, less water = higher pitch. By carefully adjusting water levels, you can tune each glass to a specific note and play melodies. This demonstrates the direct relationship between vibrating mass and frequency!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.
skill_explanation.creativity: Combining ideas in unexpected ways shows innovative thinking.

choices.label: B. A water glass xylophone produces different pitches because the water itself vibrates at different frequencies depending on the amount
choices.feedback: 💡 When you TAP a glass, it is the GLASS that vibrates, not the water. The water adds mass to the vibrating glass, slowing it down. Interestingly, when you RUB the rim with a wet finger, the glass vibrates differently and the water acts as a damper. The vibrating object is always the glass itself — the water modifies how the glass vibrates.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. Making an instrument louder requires using more expensive materials, because cheap materials cannot produce loud sounds
choices.feedback: 💡 Loudness has nothing to do with material cost! You can make a quiet vibration louder by attaching the vibrating object to a resonance chamber (like a hollow box). A rubber band stretched over an open box sounds much louder than one stretched between your fingers, because the box amplifies the vibrations by making a larger volume of air vibrate.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: D. Homemade instruments can never be properly tuned because precise tuning requires factory-built equipment and professional tools
choices.feedback: 💡 Homemade instruments can be tuned very precisely! By adjusting the length, tension, or mass of the vibrating element, you control the frequency. A straw flute can be tuned by cutting to exact lengths. A water glass xylophone is tuned by adjusting water levels. Free smartphone apps can measure frequency to verify your tuning. Physics principles are the same regardless of the instrument's cost!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

rounds.situation: CRISIS! The oscilloscope is broken, the signal generator is malfunctioning, and the best microphones are missing. Someone may have borrowed them for another class without asking. The Talent Show is two weeks away and your instruments need final tuning. Ms. Hertz says: 'Real musicians and scientists deal with equipment problems all the time. How do you adapt?'
rounds.goal: Continue preparing for the Talent Show despite severe equipment problems.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Equipment fails, plans change, resources disappear. The ability to adapt and keep going is what separates successful people from those who give up.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Can you still do science without expensive equipment? How did scientists work before modern instruments existed?
rounds.image_prompt: Sound studio with broken oscilloscope, empty equipment shelf, students brainstorming alternatives, creative improvisation happening

choices.label: A. A smartphone microphone can function as a basic oscilloscope because it converts sound waves into electrical signals that can be displayed as waveforms
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A microphone contains a thin diaphragm that vibrates when sound waves hit it. These vibrations are converted into electrical signals that mirror the original sound wave. Smartphone apps can display these signals as waveforms, measure frequency, and even show frequency spectra. The technology in your pocket can replace lab equipment that cost thousands of pounds decades ago!

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.
skill_explanation.creativity: Not settling for the obvious solution builds creative problem-solving.

choices.label: B. Ultrasound is sound that is extremely loud — 'ultra' means very powerful and intense
choices.feedback: 💡 'Ultra' in ultrasound means 'beyond,' not 'powerful'! Ultrasound is sound with frequency ABOVE 20,000 Hz — beyond the upper limit of human hearing. It can be loud or quiet. Similarly, infrasound is below 20 Hz (too low for humans to hear). Ultrasound is used in medical imaging, cleaning jewellery, and sonar. Bats and dolphins use ultrasound for navigation.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: C. Noise pollution only affects people who work in factories — normal everyday noise levels cannot harm health
choices.feedback: 💡 Noise pollution affects everyone! Constant exposure to traffic noise (70-80 dB), loud music, and urban sounds causes stress, sleep disruption, increased blood pressure, and concentration problems. The WHO says environmental noise causes 12,000 premature deaths per year in Europe alone. Even moderate background noise impairs learning in schools. Noise is a serious public health issue!

skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Standing by your values even under pressure builds integrity.

choices.label: D. Soundproofing a room works by making the walls vibrate at the opposite frequency to cancel out all incoming sound
choices.feedback: 💡 You are confusing two different technologies! Passive soundproofing uses dense, absorbent materials (thick walls, foam, mass-loaded vinyl) that absorb sound energy and prevent it from passing through. ACTIVE noise cancellation (used in headphones) creates an inverted sound wave to cancel incoming noise, but this only works in small spaces and for predictable sounds.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

rounds.situation: One week before the Talent Show! Ms. Hertz gives full creative freedom: 'Use everything you know about sound to create something that will amaze, educate, and entertain. Think beyond instruments — what else can sound do? Noise cancellation? Sound art? Acoustic illusions?' The studio buzzes with final preparations.
rounds.goal: Push creativity and knowledge to create an innovative sound project.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: Innovation is connecting things that have not been connected before. What happens when you combine sound physics with art? Or with technology? Or with helping people?
rounds.reflection_prompt: What is the most surprising thing you learned about sound this semester? How could you use that knowledge to help someone?
rounds.image_prompt: Student surrounded by instruments and sound equipment, sketching innovative project design, creative energy, prototypes on table, excited expression

choices.label: A. Active noise-cancelling headphones work by detecting incoming sound and producing an inverted wave (shifted by half a wavelength) that destructively interferes, cancelling the noise
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ When two waves of equal amplitude meet and one is shifted by exactly half a wavelength (180°), the peaks of one wave align with the troughs of the other. They cancel out, producing silence — this is destructive interference. ANC headphones use tiny microphones to detect external noise, a processor to calculate the inverted wave, and speakers to play it. The result: remarkable noise reduction!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.
skill_explanation.creativity: Thinking outside the box leads to more original solutions.

choices.label: B. The Doppler effect means that all moving objects produce sound, even if they are not vibrating
choices.feedback: 💡 The Doppler effect does not create sound — it changes the PITCH of existing sound! When an ambulance approaches you, sound waves get compressed (higher frequency = higher pitch). When it moves away, waves get stretched (lower frequency = lower pitch). That is why the siren seems to change note as it passes you: 'neeee-NAWWW.' The object must already be producing sound for the Doppler effect to occur.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: C. Soundproof rooms are completely silent inside because the walls absorb 100% of all sound energy
choices.feedback: 💡 Even the best anechoic chambers (rooms designed to absorb almost all sound) are not perfectly silent! They absorb about 99.9% of sound, but inside them you can hear your own heartbeat, blood flowing, and even a faint ringing from your nervous system. The background noise level in the quietest room on Earth (Microsoft's anechoic chamber) is -20.6 dB. True zero sound is practically impossible.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. Two identical speakers playing the same sound will always make it exactly twice as loud because the sound energies simply add together
choices.feedback: 💡 It depends on the POSITION of the listener! If the sound waves from both speakers arrive perfectly in sync (peaks align with peaks), you get constructive interference — louder sound. But if one wave's peaks align with the other's troughs (half wavelength difference in distance), you get destructive interference — the sounds partially CANCEL. This creates loud and quiet spots in a room.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

rounds.situation: The Talent Show is here! The auditorium is packed with students, parents, and teachers. Your homemade instruments are tuned, your demonstrations are ready, and your sound projects are on display. Ms. Hertz says: 'This is your stage. Show everyone that physics is not just equations — it is the science behind every sound they love.' How will you make your mark?
rounds.goal: Showcase your sound science knowledge and projects at the Talent Show.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Performing live is unpredictable — microphones fail, audiences are noisy, and nerves are real. Courage is not the absence of fear; it is performing despite it.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Looking back at Week 1, how has your understanding of sound changed? What would you tell a student just starting?
rounds.image_prompt: School Talent Show stage, students performing with homemade instruments, parents in audience, sound wave decorations, spotlight, trophy on side table

choices.label: A. The human ear converts sound waves into electrical nerve signals using tiny hair cells in the cochlea, which then travel to the brain for interpretation
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Sound waves enter the ear canal, vibrate the eardrum, which moves three tiny bones (hammer, anvil, stirrup) that amplify the vibrations. These reach the fluid-filled cochlea where about 15,000 hair cells bend in response to different frequencies. Each bent hair cell generates an electrical signal sent via the auditory nerve to the brain. The brain processes these signals into the sounds we recognise — music, speech, and everything else!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. The outer ear (pinna) is just for decoration and does not play any role in how we hear sounds
choices.feedback: 💡 The outer ear has an important job! Its funnel shape collects sound waves from a wide area and channels them into the ear canal, effectively amplifying sounds by 5-10 dB. The unique folds of your ear also help your brain determine WHERE a sound is coming from (above, below, in front, behind). That is why cupping your hand behind your ear helps you hear better!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. Humans can hear all sound frequencies that exist in nature — our hearing covers the complete range of possible sounds
choices.feedback: 💡 Humans hear only a tiny fraction of all sounds! Our range is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Dogs hear up to 45,000 Hz, cats up to 64,000 Hz, and bats up to 120,000 Hz. Elephants communicate using infrasound below 20 Hz that travels vast distances. Many animals hear sounds that are completely invisible to us. Our hearing range also shrinks with age — most adults cannot hear above 15,000 Hz.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: D. We can determine the direction of a sound source using just one ear, because a single ear can detect the direction of incoming sound waves
choices.feedback: 💡 We need BOTH ears to locate sound direction accurately! Your brain compares the tiny differences in when sound arrives at each ear and how loud it is in each ear. A sound from your right reaches your right ear a fraction of a millisecond before your left ear, and is slightly louder in the right ear. Your brain uses these tiny differences to calculate direction — this is called binaural hearing.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

glossary_terms.definition: A longitudinal wave created by vibrating objects that travels through a medium (solid, liquid, or gas) as a series of compressions and rarefactions.
A rapid back-and-forth movement of an object. All sounds are produced by vibrating objects — vocal cords, guitar strings, speaker cones, tuning forks.
The number of complete vibrations (cycles) per second, measured in Hertz (Hz). Higher frequency means higher pitch. Humans hear 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
The maximum displacement of a vibrating object from its rest position. Larger amplitude means louder sound. Measured in the height of the sound wave.
How high or low a sound seems to the human ear. Pitch is determined by frequency — high frequency produces high pitch, low frequency produces low pitch.
The unit used to measure sound intensity (loudness). Normal conversation is about 60 dB. Sounds above 85 dB can cause hearing damage with prolonged exposure.
A reflected sound wave that arrives at the listener's ear at least 0.1 seconds after the original sound. Requires a hard surface at least 17 meters away.
When an object vibrates at its natural frequency due to matching vibrations from another source. Small pushes at the right frequency create large vibrations.
Whole-number multiples of a fundamental frequency that occur naturally when an object vibrates. They determine the timbre (tone quality) of a sound.
The quality of a sound that distinguishes different instruments playing the same note. Determined by the unique pattern of harmonics each instrument produces.
How fast sound travels through a medium. In air at 20°C: ~343 m/s. In water: ~1500 m/s. In steel: ~5000 m/s. Sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
Sound with frequency above 20,000 Hz — too high for human ears. Used in medical imaging, sonar, and animal communication (bats, dolphins).

endings.title: Master Acoustician
endings.message: You have achieved mastery in the Sound Studio! Your understanding of acoustics is exceptional, your instruments are beautifully crafted, and your hearing safety awareness is exemplary. Ms. Hertz nominates you for the District Science Olympiad acoustics event, and your homemade instrument collection becomes a permanent school display. Sound mastery achieved!

endings.title: Skilled Sound Engineer
endings.message: You have become a skilled sound scientist with solid acoustics knowledge and good studio practices! Your Talent Show performance impressed the judges and your data collection is meticulous. Ms. Hertz says you are ready for the advanced physics program. Keep listening — there is so much more to hear!

endings.title: Steady Learner
endings.message: You completed the Sound Studio program with mixed results. Some weeks were great and others were challenging, but you persisted and learned the fundamentals of acoustics. Ms. Hertz says there is always next semester to refine your skills. Keep your ears open — sound science is everywhere!

endings.title: Struggling Student
endings.message: The Sound Studio was tough for you. Some concepts felt abstract and the instrument building was frustrating at times. But you showed up every week and never quit. Ms. Hertz says: 'The students who keep trying, even when it is hard, are the ones who eventually break through.' Your sound journey is just beginning!

endings.title: Hearing Safety Concern
endings.message: Due to repeated hearing safety violations, Ms. Hertz has restricted your access to loud equipment until you complete the Hearing Safety Certification. Hearing damage is permanent and invisible — this is the most serious safety concern in acoustics. Echo has prepared a personalized safety course for you. Protect your ears and come back stronger!

questions.question: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.explanation: Force is measured in Newtons (N), named after Sir Isaac Newton.

questions.question: What happens when balanced forces act on a stationary object?
questions.explanation: Balanced forces cancel out, so the object remains stationary.

questions.question: Friction always acts in which direction?
questions.explanation: Friction opposes the direction of motion or attempted motion.
